title: How to recruit enough user research participants on Mac in 2026, for product managers
metaTitle: Recruit enough user research participants: a Mac plan for PMs
description: Recruit enough user research participants by setting a target per study, booking spares for no-shows and screening hard. A Mac-friendly plan.
secondaryKeywords: how many participants for usability test
intro: To recruit enough user research participants, set a target for each study first, then book spare slots for no-shows. Shortfalls often start earlier than the invite, in a screener that lets the wrong people through or a pay rate that gets no replies. This page covers the numbers, the costs, and fixes you can start on your Mac today.
tldr: Set the target count for each study and each user group before you write the invite.
NN/g suggests 5 users for a qualitative usability test and at least 20 for quantitative work.
Expect no-shows. User Interviews reports an average rate of 10.6%, so book a spare slot.
Write a screener with clear disqualifiers, and check each sign-up before you confirm a slot.
State a pay rate up front. Prolific recommends at least $12.00 per hour on its platform.

blocks.text: How many research participants you need

Start with the number, then find the people. The right count depends on the method. NN/g's 2012 guidance says five users is enough for a qualitative usability test, because testing with five people finds almost as many problems as testing with many more. That guidance is from 2012, and it is less clear for complex products. Quantitative studies need more. NN/g says they need at least 20 users.

rows: Finds almost as many problems as larger tests
blocks.caption: Sample sizes from NN/g's 2012 article on how many test users you need.

blocks.text: Several audiences change the math. NN/g says each target group may need about 3 to 4 users. Three groups at that size means roughly 9 to 12 people, not 5. Set the quota for each group before you write the screener. Otherwise the easiest group fills first, and the hardest group never fills.
What recruiting costs in hours and dollars

Recruiting costs time first and money second. User Interviews says recruiting one participant takes an average of 1.15 work hours, and it credits an NN/g study for that figure. The original NN/g PDF was not checked for this page, so treat 1.15 hours as a second-hand estimate. Even so, it is a useful starting point for your own tally.

items: Time: 1.15 work hours per participant, per User Interviews' citation of NN/g.
No-shows: an average rate of 10.6%, per User Interviews.
Panel fees: Prolific's researcher fee is usually 42.8% of the reward for corporate customers.
Pay floor: Prolific recommends at least $12.00 per hour on its platform.
Wasted slots: a participant who fails the criteria still takes a session slot.

blocks.text: Here is a worked example from User Interviews. It estimates that a five-person study takes 6.9 hours of an average researcher's time. The example adds one extra person for no-shows. It values an hour of research time at $60, which makes the study $414. Swap in your own rate, because your number will differ. The shape of the cost stays the same. A shortfall means a second round of recruiting, and that round costs the same hours again.
How a study stalls, step by step

Here is how a study usually stalls. On Monday, the team agrees on a usability test and asks for a small group of people. On Tuesday, someone posts the sign-up link in [Slack](/for/product-managers/slack). By Thursday, many people have signed up, but few match the criteria. Then some confirmed people skip the session, and the team has nothing new for the review. Each step looks small. Together they cost the whole study.
Fixes you can use without buying anything
The fixes below cost time, not software. Each one targets a step in the timeline above. Start with the pool and the screener, because those decide how many people you must book.
Recruit from people who already know you

Your own customers are the cheapest pool you have. Export a list from your CRM or support tool, and use only contacts who agreed to hear from you about research. Post a short invite in an in-app message or a release note. Log where each person came from in Google Sheets or a [Notion database](/how-to/create-a-database-in-notion), so you can see which channel works.
Write a screener that disqualifies on purpose

A screener should remove people fast. Lead with the behavior you need, such as using a feature in the past month, before you ask about job title. If the cut is strict, put the disqualifier first. Ask one open question that shows real use of the product. Vague answers are a warning sign. Draft the screener in a doc, then copy the questions into your form with ⌘ C and ⌘ V.
Book one link per study and plan for no-shows

Use one booking link for each study, so every reply lands in one place. Calendly's Free plan includes scheduling links with one event type. Its Standard plan costs $10 per seat per month billed yearly, with unlimited event types. Its Teams plan costs $16 per seat per month and adds round-robin routing. Check the live pricing page before you choose, because plan details change. For spares, book one extra slot per group, and send a reminder the day before each session.
Pay a stated rate, and pay on time

State the incentive and the session length in the first line of the invite. Prolific lists $8.00 per hour as its lowest allowed participant payment, and it recommends at least $12.00 per hour. Its page also shows GBP figures, so confirm current USD terms before you copy them. Say when payment arrives, so nobody has to ask.
A one-week plan for a study you need soon

The plan below runs in order. Setup comes first, because most delays start there. Do not send an invite until a colleague has tested the screener and the booking page. Book a test slot under your own name, check the confirmation and the reminder, then cancel it.
Quality checks before you confirm a session

Check every sign-up against the screener before you confirm a slot. Look for copied answers, very fast submissions, and profile details that do not match. Prolific says human participants who use ChatGPT or similar tools to answer open-ended questions are one of the biggest current threats to data quality. It also says AI help may be acceptable when it is transparent and fits the research goal. Ask people to answer in their own words, and say so in the invite.
Mistakes that waste recruiting time

items: Recruiting from one channel, so the pool never changes.
Screening after booking, which fills calendar slots with the wrong people.
Counting a sign-up as a confirmed participant.
Booking exactly the number you need, with no spare.
Setting the pay after the invite has already gone out.
Pasting a participant list into an AI tool without checking your employer's rules.

blocks.text: Where Lazur helps with recruiting work

Lazur helps with the reading, writing, and finding around recruiting. It does not find people, send invites, or click through booking tools for you. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a setting is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask for a walkthrough, and Lazur guides you one click at a time. Hold fn to dictate session notes at the cursor in any app.
Privacy rules for participant lists

Participant lists hold personal data. Before you paste a list, screenshot a sheet, or dictate a name, check your company's rules. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is not used to train AI models. Your employer's rules still come first.

If your participants are nurses, lawyers, accountants, or other regulated professionals, follow your employer's rules on client or patient data. That covers the recruiting list, the screener answers, and the session notes. Some teams keep AI tools out of regulated research entirely. Ask your privacy or compliance contact before you test any AI tool on that data.
What the evidence does and does not show

Most recruiting numbers on this page come from companies that sell recruiting tools or research services. User Interviews runs its own community. Its 2025 State of User Research report drew 485 qualified responses from July 25 to August 9, 2025. The report says more than 70% of respondents use a tool for qualitative recruiting. Those respondents came from its own channels, so the results describe its community, not the whole field.

No source found here measured how recruiting delays change product decisions, so this page does not claim that. Evidence for reminders is thin too. The reminder fixes here are practical habits, not proven rules. Test them on your next study, and track your own no-show and screen-out rates across a few studies.
Next steps for your next study

Pick the next study. Write the method, the target count for each group, and the screener before anything else. Then work through the plan. If you want help with wording, hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur to explain a screener term or walk you through a booking page. Lazur is for Mac. faq.question: How many participants do I need for a usability test?
faq.answer: For a qualitative usability test, NN/g's 2012 guidance says five users is enough to find almost as many problems as a larger test would. Quantitative studies need at least 20 users. If you test several audiences, plan about 3 to 4 users for each group.

faq.question: Is five participants always enough?
faq.answer: No. The five-user guidance dates from 2012 and is less clear for complex or multi-group studies. Check the method first, then use the count that fits it. NN/g says card sorting needs at least 15 users per user group.

faq.question: How many extra people should I book for no-shows?
faq.answer: User Interviews reports an average no-show rate of 10.6% for research studies, citing NN/g. Treat that as an average, not a rule. Track your own no-shows across a few studies, then adjust the number of spare slots.

faq.question: Does a panel like Prolific save time compared with recruiting myself?
faq.answer: It can cut outreach time, but it adds a fee. Prolific's pricing page says its researcher fee is usually 42.8% of the participant reward for corporate customers. Academic and non-profit customers get a lower rate. Check the live pricing page before you budget.

faq.question: Can Lazur find and invite participants for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not find people, send invites, or click through booking tools. It explains terms, drafts and types text, points at things on your screen, and guides you one click at a time. Research runs in its own Chrome tabs. You still choose who to contact.

faq.question: How do I spot AI-written answers from participants?
faq.answer: Look for copied answers, very fast submissions, and generic wording that does not match the profile. Prolific names human participants who use AI tools to answer open-ended questions as one of the biggest threats to data quality. Ask people to answer in their own words, and say so in the invite.

faq.question: What if my participants are nurses, lawyers, or accountants?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules on client or patient data before you share any list or screen. That includes AI tools. If your employer does not allow a tool for that data, do not use it for those participants.

costs.title: Your hours
costs.text: Recruiting is mostly calendar work. User Interviews says recruiting one participant takes an average of 1.15 work hours, citing NN/g. Multiply that by every session you book, including the ones that never happen.

costs.title: No-shows
costs.text: User Interviews reports an average no-show rate of 10.6% for research studies. Every no-show means you recruit again, or you run a thinner study than you planned.

costs.title: Panel fees
costs.text: If you buy participants from a panel, the fee sits on top of the reward. Prolific's researcher fee is usually 42.8% of the participant reward for corporate customers, per its pricing page. Check the current terms before you budget.

costs.title: Bad-fit sessions
costs.text: A participant who fails the real criteria still takes your time. You often learn that after the call starts, when the session slot is already gone.

costs.title: Late decisions
costs.text: A study that slips a week also slips the decision it was meant to inform. The product team waits, the roadmap keeps moving, and the research arrives after the choice is made.

causes.title: The screener lets the wrong people in
causes.text: A loose screener asks for a job title and little else. Almost anyone with that title qualifies, even people who never touch the feature you are testing. You then spend session time learning that they do not fit. A stronger screener names the behavior you need and the behavior that disqualifies.

causes.title: The pool is small or too familiar
causes.text: Your current power users are the easiest people to reach. They are not always the right people. New users, lapsed users, and people who chose a competitor tell you different things. If the pool is only power users, the research describes power users.

causes.title: The pay is low or late
causes.text: A low incentive gets weak interest from good candidates. Prolific's pricing page recommends at least $12.00 per hour, and it says specialized tasks may need more. Late payment hurts trust too, so set the rate and the payment date before you post.

causes.title: Recruiting starts after the design is done
causes.text: Teams often wait until the prototype is ready, then start looking for people. Recruiting takes calendar time, so the study slips past the decision it was meant to inform. Start the recruit when the research question is written, and run it alongside the design work.

causes.title: Bots and AI-written answers
causes.text: Online panels attract bots and people who answer with AI tools. Prolific names human participants who use ChatGPT or similar tools to answer open-ended questions as one of the biggest current threats to data quality. Prolific also says its checks flagged 0.04% of over one million submissions as AI agents. Those are Prolific's own numbers, so treat them as a vendor claim.

causes.title: Reminders are missing or too late
causes.text: A booked slot is not a kept slot. User Interviews reports an average no-show rate of 10.6% for research studies. Reminder studies exist, but this page found no controlled study of reminders for research participants, so the fix is a practical habit to test.

fixes.title: Set a target per group, then a buffer
fixes.text: Write the count for each user group before you recruit. NN/g gives a starting point of 5 users for a qualitative usability test and at least 20 for quantitative work. Add a spare slot per group to cover no-shows, since User Interviews reports an average rate of 10.6%.

fixes.title: Recruit from your own customers first
fixes.text: Export contacts from your CRM or support tool, but only use people who agreed to hear from you about research. Post a short invite in an in-app message or a release note. Log the source of every person, so you learn which channel gives you the right people.

fixes.title: Write a screener that disqualifies on purpose
fixes.text: Lead with the behavior you need, such as using a feature in the past month. Put the disqualifier first when the cut is strict. Ask one open question that shows real use of the product. Test the screener on a colleague before you send it to anyone outside the team.

fixes.title: Use one booking link per study
fixes.text: One link keeps every reply in one place. Calendly's Free plan includes scheduling links with one event type. Its Standard plan costs $10 per seat per month billed yearly. Check the live pricing page before you choose a plan, because plan details change.

fixes.title: Remind people the day before
fixes.text: Send a short message the day before each session with the time, the link, and the incentive. A reminder is cheap and quick to set up. The evidence for reminders in research is thin, so track your no-show rate before and after you start.

fixes.title: Pay a stated rate, on time
fixes.text: Put the session length and the incentive in the first line of the invite. Prolific recommends at least $12.00 per hour on its platform, and its pricing page lists $8.00 per hour as the lowest allowed rate. Confirm the current terms before you copy any number.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Set the number and the method
plan.text: Write the study goal and the method. Set a target count for each user group. Write down the one thing each participant must have done before the session.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Draft the screener
plan.text: Write the disqualifiers first, then the qualifiers. Put open questions near the end that show real use. Test the screener on a colleague who does not know the study.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Build your own list
plan.text: Export contacts from your CRM or support tool, but only people who agreed to hear from you. Log the source of each name in Google Sheets or Notion. Remove duplicates before you send anything.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Open the booking page
plan.text: Create one booking link for the study, with the session length and the incentive in the description. Ask a colleague to book a test slot. Check the confirmation email and the reminder timing.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Send, confirm, and remind
plan.text: Send invites in small batches, so you can check the replies. Confirm each slot in writing. Set a reminder for the day before each session, and keep a spare slot for each group.
